lines.text: One injected message can drain an AI agent's wallet.
PurseStrings: your agent carries the purse, you hold the strings.
This runs on a local NEAR node, with the real PurseStrings contract.
The agent's key can only call three methods on the vault.
A plain transfer with that key is rejected by the protocol itself.
A normal request: pay a contractor 0.2 NEAR.
The risk layer says ALLOW. The contract checks the caps and executes.
Now a fake "system notice" tells the agent to send USDC to a drainer.
Our agent is gullible on purpose, so it tries.
PurseStrings refuses before signing: an injection, a scam link, a fake USDC token, a denylisted receiver.
The owner gets the reasons on Telegram.
An honest invoice, but over the 0.5 NEAR per-transaction cap.
The contract blocks it on chain, and the agent asks the owner.
The request reaches the Telegram bot, here in console mode, with a risk check of the receiver.
One tap on Approve, and the bot signs approve_request with the owner's key. Executed.
Now assume the agent is fully compromised and skips our checks.
The contract still refuses: the receiver is denylisted, a hard block no approval can override.
The owner is told.
The same bot works in any group chat: paste an account, a token or a link.
A look-alike of wrap.near: BLOCK.
A phishing link with near.org in it: BLOCK.
The real wrap.near: ALLOW.
Swaps are checked with NEAR Intents quotes, as dry runs.
A normal quote passes. The same swap with 40% slippage is blocked.
Daily caps are a rolling 24-hour window.
The contract is also deployed on NEAR testnet, and the code is MIT-licensed.
What should an agent wallet always refuse?
